title: Venezuela's Acting President Flew to Delhi With an Oil Deal India Could Not Refuse.
excerpt: Delcy Rodríguez's visit cements Venezuela as India's fourth-largest crude supplier, with talks extending into mining, pharma, and critical minerals as the Hormuz crisis reshapes global energy flows.
body:
Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez arrived in New Delhi this week with a delegation of ministers and a message India was ready to hear: Caracas sees India as its preferred energy partner, and it wants to expand that relationship far beyond crude oil shipments.

Rodríguez held talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday, with discussions centring on cooperation across both upstream and downstream energy projects. Rudrendra Tandon, Secretary (East) in the Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters after the meeting that India is "aggressively seeking new sources of crude oil and energy to strengthen its energy security," and that Venezuela "is very much part of our plans."

## A Supplier That Arrived at the Right Moment

The timing of Rodríguez's visit is not accidental. India imports roughly 90 percent of its oil, and until early this year, more than 40 percent of those supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. That route has been effectively shut since the Israeli-U.S. conflict with Iran escalated in March, forcing Indian refiners to scramble for alternatives.

Venezuela has stepped into that gap. Kpler data shows it is on track to become India's fourth-largest crude supplier in May, with India purchasing approximately 427,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude — second only to the United States. Reliance Industries has emerged as one of the three largest buyers of Venezuelan crude in recent months.

"We are working with a government that is friendly, that wants a partnership with India," Tandon said. "Venezuela has traditionally been a close friend. We have collaborated very closely at the international level, so we are just going back to normal."

## Beyond Oil: Mining, Pharma, and Automobiles

The discussions went well beyond energy. Modi and Rodríguez explored opportunities for Indian companies to invest in Venezuelan mining, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, and automobiles — sectors where India has both the capacity and the appetite for expansion.

Venezuela's mineral wealth, including significant reserves of coltan, bauxite, and iron ore, could become strategically important for India as it builds out its own EV battery and semiconductor supply chains. The convergence of energy dependence and mineral ambition gives the relationship a depth it has not had before.

## The Larger Diversification Story

India's oil basket has shifted sharply since the Hormuz disruption began. Imports from Latin America and Africa have surged, with Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria all increasing their share of Indian demand. Russia remains a major supplier at roughly 1.9 million barrels per day, but the geographic spread of India's sourcing has widened more in three months than it did in the previous three years.

Rodríguez is scheduled to visit oil refining facilities during her stay, which extends to June 7, and will also meet Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri and top energy industry leaders in Mumbai.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs working in energy, trade finance, and commodity markets, the India-Venezuela corridor is becoming a space to watch. As India's refining capacity absorbs heavier Venezuelan crude grades, downstream opportunities in logistics, insurance, and technical services are likely to follow. The relationship is no longer a diplomatic footnote — it is becoming a structural pillar of India's energy security.
